blocks.text: Two Images Are Better Than One
In Frozen Features , American photographer and publisher Jason Fulford overlays his negatives at random. From each collision emerges a third image, forging its own syntax.
By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Jason Fulford.

A knife plunged into a white table, its shadow stretching long as an accusation, and around it, scattered like coins on a counter, watch faces stripped of their hands. Welcome to Frozen Features : a book where every image is already double, where meaning surfaces in the gap, sharp and immediate, before any explanation.

Jason Fulford holds ten thousand digitized negatives, thirty years of images kept in envelopes, boxed, stored in a cabinet. Last year, he began overlaying them at random, two negatives at a time, to see what their meeting might produce. From roughly a thousand pairs generated by chance, he kept a few hundred, then spent two days with Sarah Chaplin Espenon, editor at Loose Joints, whittling them down to fifty-four: purely intuitive work.

Only the combinations that “sing” survive. Charles Goslin, his graphic design professor, used to collect obituaries from The New York Times featuring people who had led double lives, two improbable existences fused into one. He asked his students to distill that duality into a single logo. Jason Fulford never stopped practicing that exercise.

For the photographer, two images placed side by side alter each other: from their encounter emerges an additional layer of meaning. Ferdinand de Saussure, the father of modern linguistics, put it this way: the value of a sign arises not from its own content, but from its difference from all the others.

A man seen from behind paints a madonna in watercolor against the New Mexico sky: without the straight road stretching beneath his brush, without the arid desert around him, the figure is nothing. With it, she becomes an apparition. Jason Fulford forges morphemes, minimal units whose meaning stays suspended, waiting for encounter.

Frozen Features opens with a line from American photographer Barbara Morgan, written in 1942: “Modern life is photomontage. In our thoughts and feelings, the images vital to us move together, skipping over the factual detail.” Jason Fulford takes her at her word, then goes further: he surrenders syntax to chance in order to surface the grammar buried beneath conscious thought.

TThese photographs each existed independently, made across thirty years of practice, yet were never intended to meet. In his address to the reader, Jason Fulford writes: “A metaphysical slot machine scoured my subconscious & fed it back to me, two memories at a time.” A fragmented face in a rearview mirror while a freight train barrels past in the background: two moments that never crossed paths now share the same second, and time ceases to be chronological. It becomes stratigraphic.

“The only way for them to last is for them to never fully be resolved,” says Jason Fulford — and one thinks of what American art historian Benjamin Buchloh wrote about Gerhard Richter’s paintings: vexations , puzzles that seem to promise a solution yet resist every attempt to reach one.

Roland Barthes, the French theorist of the image and founding father of modern semiology, called punctum that detail which pricks in a photograph and wounds, in the literal sense: a puncture, a breach in the gaze. Jason Fulford makes images with a double punctum : a toy dinosaur skeleton dissolving into the pink facade of a building at night, two simultaneous wounds contaminating each other. It is, as Loose Joints puts it, work that is “felt before it’s understood.”

Jason Fulford puts it plainly: “I always try to make work that the reader finishes.” And so Frozen Features is not a closed book: it is a half-written score, a sentence missing its verb. This is where the reader comes in. Two images are better than one, granted. But two images plus a gaze: that’s a complete sentence. Yours to make.
Frozen Features by Jason Fulford is published by Loose Joints , 104 pages, 54 color plates, $68.
